notes.explains: We take the white pieces and open with the king's pawn; Black answers symmetrically with e5, a reply we haven't met in a while. Into it we've been alternating two systems — the Vienna and the Four Knights Scotch — and today we steer for the Scotch.
The king's knight develops to f3, the first step into the Four Knights.
Black brings a knight to c6, and we mirror with the queen's knight to c3. Both sides simply develop the knights first; once Black adds the knight to f6, we're set to break in the centre.
Black plays the last knight to f6, and now the point of the system: d4, striking the e5-pawn with every piece already developed.

Instead of resolving the centre, Black steps the bishop to b4 — a rare sideline here that we've almost never faced, and a touch passive. The main road would have been the capture on d4, we retake with the knight, and only then the bishop to b4. This is playable, but it leaves White a small edge.

We must not grab with the pawn: after taking on e5 the knight springs to e4 and hits our c3-knight. Instead we push d5, seizing space and locking the centre. Black sometimes steers into this very structure with the black pieces, because it forces White to close up and gives the second player something to play for — though positionally Black is simply more cramped.
Black swings the knight from c6 to e7, heading for g6.

We develop the bishop to d3, defending e4 and drawing the sting from any jump to e4 — with that square covered, the knight can no longer hit our c3-knight with tempo. And we're untroubled by a capture on c3.
Black bolsters the centre with d6. We're not afraid of the trade on c3: yes, it damages our pawns, but in return we get the bishop pair and the chance to buttress the centre with c4.
We castle kingside. We could also slip in h3 to discourage the bishop coming to g4, but that pin is toothless here — Black's pieces are too passive to make anything of it.
Black captures on c3. Had he tried the bishop to g4 instead, we'd have answered h3 to chase it back, and could even have followed with g4.
We recapture with the b-pawn, accepting the doubled c-pawns in exchange for the bishop pair and a broad centre.

Black lands the knight on g6 — the correct setup in this closed centre. And that's the lesson of these positions: when the centre is locked, the worth of any single move drops. Move orders turn flexible; what matters is reaching the right setup and the right plan, not the exact sequence.
We begin with h3, denying the bishop the g4-square. In a closed position the emphasis shifts from the individual move to the overall aim.
Black castles. Another strong move for us is c4, reinforcing the d5-pawn.
We play c4, cementing d5 and hinting at a future c5 break.
Black plays b6, holding the queenside confidently. We simply keep developing.

The bishop to g5 would catch the eye, but Black just plays h6 and shoos it away — so we settle for the bishop to e3, completing our development. Now we can turn to the side where we hold the edge: the kingside. On the queenside we'll never get in c5; on the kingside we have more force gathered.
Black centralizes the queen to e7. Our development is done, and the extra pieces sit on the kingside — that's where the game will be decided, and we have several promising ideas there.
We tuck the king to h2 — a quiet move with a double purpose that will show itself: it is at once prophylactic and aggressive.
Black lunges the knight to h5, aiming for f4. Now the point of the king move surfaces: it is prophylaxis against exactly this, and our reply is g3.

We meet it with g3. This is only safe because the king stands on h2 — otherwise the h3-pawn could fall to a sacrifice; with the king there, that door is shut. And why did Black go to h5 at all? He is angling for f5, but it fails tactically: after f5 we take, the bishop retakes, we take again, the rook recaptures, and g4 at the very end forks the rook and the knight. There is a hidden cost to the knight sitting on h5 too — our queen x-rays it straight through our own f3-knight, so we can lift that knight, which we wanted to do anyway to prepare f4, and chase the h5-knight back to f6, gaining a tempo on our own plan.

Black retreats the knight to f6. With the knight back, we press on — but carefully. Play the knight to d2 now and the queen comes to d7, forcing g4; and g4 fatally weakens the f4-square, killing the very break we're preparing.
So we play the knight back to g1, preemptively: it guards h3 and clears the path to prepare f4. We're not ready to play f4 just yet.

Black plays the knight to d7 — pre-moved, so he never saw the queen-to-d7 resource. But committing to a plan doesn't mean closing your eyes: you must read how the opponent's move reshapes the position. And f4 still carries a serious flaw — after f4, the capture on f4, and g-takes-f4, Black strikes back with f5, and once the centre opens our e3-bishop falls under the queen's x-ray, so taking on f5 walks into tactics that leave our king badly exposed. Piling another defender on f4 with the knight to e2 isn't the cure; the cure is to shield the bishop first — but there's no time, because after the queen to d2 the knight swings to c5 and the break fails anyway, since capturing on f4 leaves our e4-pawn hanging.

So we change tack — shelve f4 for now and open a second front with h4. It doesn't come from nowhere: the g3-pawn supports the advance. Worried about the sacrifice on h4? The knight takes, g-takes, queen-takes-h4 with check, and we simply slide the king to g2 — and here the knight on g1 earns its keep, guarding h3, so once Black's d7-knight moves there's no check on h3. The upside of h4: the straightforward h5 next, shoving the g6-knight to the rim; the knight on g1 is freed and the h3-pawn stops being a worry — the queen can still reach h3, but no longer with a capture — and we may win the g5-square as an outpost for the bishop.

Black jumps the knight to c5. A healthy positional move for us either way — and we haven't wholly abandoned f4, though with the pawn heading to h5 it's far less likely: once h5 is in, an f4 break would only gut our own king, so we'd allow it only under perfect circumstances. Black is playing this very well.
We push h5. This can hardly hurt — and it looks like the knight is more or less forced to h8, buried on the edge.

Instead Black finds the knight to f4 — I'll admit I missed it. Does it work? The lines run deep: it holds tactically to a draw by perpetual, but it doesn't win. And crucially we don't have to take it — we can capture on c5 first, which may be the real solution.
We take on c5 first with the bishop. Now the queen to h4 is not mate, because the g3-pawn covers that square.
Black recaptures with the b-pawn on c5. There was a very specific reason to take on c5 first.
Now g-takes-f4 works — though it's razor-thin, move-for-move calculation where you get it exactly right or lose ground.
Black checks with the queen on h4.

We step the king to g2. The looming idea is the queen to f3 — a genuinely frightening move; there may be a hidden win for Black I can't see, but move-for-move I believe we hold. Behind these choices sit the details: if the bishop comes to g4 now, we take on e5, and the bishop to h3 only looks like it traps the queen — our knight swings in, takes the bishop and defends the queen at once; and if Black tries a perpetual with the queen to g5 and back to h4, that same knight blocks on h3.
We push d4 and offer the Scotch Gambit.
Black takes the pawn on d4.

We develop the bishop to c4 — this is the Scotch Gambit, a hybrid of the Scotch and the Italian. It's a genuinely dangerous, grandmaster-approved weapon, and a fine alternative if you like the Evans Gambit; at club level its traps bring quick wins.

Black plays d6, a solid, slightly passive choice that sidesteps the gambit's traps — a line playable with the black pieces too, leaving a marginally worse game. The point of the early bishop, as in the Italian, is access to the g5-square, where a knight or bishop is a key resource in many lines.

We recapture on d4 with the knight, regaining the gambit pawn and opening lines. White has the pleasant side — better central control, the bishop raking from c4 as in a good Scotch, and the sacrificed pawn already back.
Black develops the knight to f6. Should we fear a capture on d4 that drops the queen into the centre?

We develop the knight to c3. No — a capture on d4 wouldn't scare us: Black has no second knight on b8 to come to c6 and harass the queen, so it would just be well-placed for us to strike at. This is the same solid setup you can reach through a Philidor move order.
Black tucks the bishop to e7 — very solid, the d6-pawn restraining our e-pawn. Don't lunge at Black's throat here.
We castle. Rather than force matters, nurture the edge: complete development and enjoy White's space and well-placed pieces.

Black castles. Now a deceptively tricky moment. f4 is premature with the queen undeveloped, and the natural bishop moves to e3 or g5 each walk into tactics: after the bishop to e3, the knight to g4 is annoying, and worse, the shot on e4 — because ...d5 then regains the piece and forces the mass trades we're trying to avoid.
The move that permanently removes that idea is the bishop to b3: it drops the bishop onto a defended square, out of reach of a future ...d5 pawn fork.
We take the white pieces and steer for the Glek System.
Black's knight comes to f6 and we answer with the knight to c3, heading into the Four Knights.
We fianchetto with g3 — the move that defines the Glek.
Black chooses the bishop to e7.
Black plays d6 — a modest, passive setup: nothing outright wrong with it, but it lets us do whatever we like.
We castle.

Black develops the bishop to e6, which tempts d4 — but in the Glek be careful with that push. Not because Black might trade everything on d4 (that suits us fine), but because of ...Bg4: even at the cost of a tempo it hangs the d4-pawn and can force us to close with d5, betraying the whole spirit of the system. Ducking it by taking on e5 is a dull move that invites mass exchanges.
So instead of an immediate d4 we play h3, keeping our options open and preparing d4 under better circumstances (the quiet d3 is also available).
Black replies h6 — and now d4 will work.
We push d4. It works like a charm: it threatens a fork and all but forces Black to release the tension.
Black captures on d4 and we recapture with the knight.
The knights come off on d4 and our queen recaptures, landing us a very pleasant position — but we mustn't forget the h3-pawn.
Black centralizes the queen to d7.
We step the king to h2 to defend h3. Careful here: many players castle queenside instead and simply hang the a7-pawn — a mistake I've seen again and again.

Black lunges h5, trying for a kingside attack — but knowing the system, you see it isn't one: Black threatens nothing. To ...h4 we simply push g4, and a sac like ...Bxg4 is futile — the position is too passive, there aren't enough attackers, and our king is far too safe.
Notice the bishop on e6 has run out of squares — so f4 comes naturally, grabbing space and setting a very nasty threat.
Black plays c5. And yes, White's plan is genuinely hard to meet: as long as we deny the bishop its escape, f5 is a monstrous threat.
That tells us where the queen belongs — d3, guarding the c4-square and discouraging ...b5 (which wasn't dangerous anyway, since e5 would answer it).
Black plays g6 — but it doesn't stop f5.
We play f5. The game is effectively over — after the coming exchanges the e6-bishop is trapped.
Black takes with the g-pawn on f5.
We recapture with the e-pawn on f5 — the bishop is trapped and our position fully open.
Black tries c4, but it changes nothing. We could lift the queen to f3, but simpler is to capture on e6.
We take on e6, hitting the queen on d7.
Black recaptures on e6. Now reposition the queen toward f3 — but note, with the king on h2 under an x-ray, keep an eye on a sudden ...Ng4 check; in the right setting it can be very nasty.
Here the check would be harmless — our king just steps to g1 — but there's no reason to invite it. Instead the queen goes to f5, more to the point, and now the queen trade can't be avoided.
Black castles long. There's no reason for us to capture on e6 ourselves — it would only repair Black's pawns and help build a central chain.
So instead we play the bishop to g5, hitting the knight — this should win further material, since after a queen trade on f5 and the rook recapture the pin tells.
Black tries the knight to g4 with check, but we simply take it — the g1-square is free.
We capture on g4.
Black checks on g4 and we tuck the king to g1.
Black recaptures the bishop on g5.
We don't need the queen — we just take the bishop back on g5, staying up two minor pieces. Always watch the a7–g1 diagonal, but with no checks there our king is perfectly safe.
Black tucks the king to b8. We're up two pieces — time to bring a rook to the centre.
The rook swings to e1, heading for the seventh rank — and the capture on f7 is coming. It's over.
Black plays the queen to d7.
We plant the rook on e7.
Black's queen retreats to c8.
Simpler than taking on b7 is to double on f7.
Black pushes d5.
We take on b7 with check, winning the queen and mopping up everything loose.
The queens come off, we recapture with check, and the bishop check on d5 opens the hunt for the king.
A check on f6 herds the king forward.
The king walks to c5. Chasing the very fastest mate here is fiddly.
So don't agonize over the quickest path — just keep checking and the mate arrives. We check on c6.
The king steps to d4 and the knight checks from b5 — Black walks right into it.

The king goes to e5 and the queen delivers mate on e6. The takeaway on the Glek: you don't have to prevent ...Bg4 in general — if Black plays it, h3 and then g4 just shove the bishop to a passive square. It's ONLY when you intend d4 that stopping ...Bg4 matters, because d4 ...Bg4 forces the closed, King's-Indian-like structure you don't want from a Glek. If you'd rather not bother with h3 or d4 at all, the quiet d3 setup is fine — it just doesn't squeeze the most from the position. Against this passive setup White simply does everything he wants: fianchetto, seize the centre, and Black stays paralysed until he can free himself with ...d5.
We meet the queen-pawn setup with the knight to f6; White stakes out c4 and d4, and we're heading into a King's Indian.
We fianchetto with g6, and White develops the knight to f3.
The bishop lands on g7, and White goes for the fianchetto too with g3 — one of the most respected tries against the King's Indian.
We reply with the classical d6.
White completes the fianchetto, the bishop settling on g2.
We castle, and White castles.
We pick the classical setup — the queen's knight to d7. Easy to learn, easy to understand, and what I play in my serious blitz.
White develops the bishop to g5, eyeing our knight — though the e7-pawn means it's no real pin.
The knight to d7 is at least as common as the knight to c6 here — c6 invites d5 with tempo, and d7 sidesteps that.
And the whole idea of the d7-knight is to prepare the e5 break.
So the bishop to g5 shows up — common at the lower levels, but not really threatening, since it isn't hitting anything it can win on f6.
We ask the bishop the polite question with h6.
White hands over the bishop pair, capturing on f6.
We recapture on f6 with the knight — flexibility. With White's dark-squared bishop gone, White brings the other knight to c3.
We carve open the long diagonal with c5.
White clamps the centre with d5 — now it's a Benoni structure, and that long diagonal is beautiful.
The bishop comes to f5, preparing the knight to e4 — a very standard maneuver.
White plays the knight to d2 to stop e4. It's a good move, but if White ever pushes e4, that d2-knight is left without a clear home.
We play a6, planning to drop the bishop calmly back to d7.
White grabs the centre with e4, and the bishop retreats to d7, ready for the classic Benoni break, b5.
White reroutes with the knight to f3, preparing to counter-strike with e5.
We stop it with the knight to g4, heading for the e5 outpost.
White pokes with h3, and the knight lands on e5, going for a trade.
White takes on e5, and we recapture with the bishop, capturing on e5 — this bishop is our main asset.
White lunges g4, doing nothing at all against our real plan of b5.
We push b5. Some would grab dark squares with g5 here, but that would be a serious mistake.
White takes on b5, and we recapture with the a-pawn, capturing on b5.
White brings the queen to d2, hitting the h6-pawn.
Rather than g5, we keep piling on with b4.
White retreats the knight to e2.
The bishop swings to b5 — indirectly defending h6, since grabbing that pawn would now achieve nothing.
White lifts the rook to e1, reinforcing the threat.
We tuck the bishop back to g7, which also stops f4 coming with tempo.
White plants the knight on f4. Back to the queenside: c4 is tempting, but it would drop the b4-pawn.
So we prepare it and beef up the queenside with the queen to a5.
White throws in h4.
Now we step on the gas with c4.
White pushes h5.
We could close the kingside with g5, but there's no need yet — instead we play c3.
White captures on c3.
The greedy move is to grab material, but we recapture on c3 with the b-pawn — very much in the King's Indian spirit.
White drops the queen to c2.
Now we shut the kingside with g5 so our king never gets pried open.
White reroutes the knight to d3. Time for the final stage on the queenside.
There's the quiet bishop to a4, but the Soviet way is the queen to a4, offering the trade.
White takes, and we recapture with the rook, capturing on a4 — the queen trade itself is our weapon, and White's position collapses.
White scrambles the knight back to c1.
The passed pawn marches to c2.
White tries the knight to b3, but the rook on a1 is now trapped.
We collect the exchange, capturing on a1 with the bishop.
White recaptures on a1 with the rook.
We bring the other rook in — to a8, not c8 — forcing White's knight back to c1.
White's rook retreats to c1, and we snatch the pawn, capturing on a2 with the rook — the rook to b4 and b1 was cleanest, but this wins too.
White's king steps to h2.
We swing the back rook down to a3, doubling on the third rank.
White tries the knight to d4, and the bishop comes to d3, guarding the c2-pawn.
White lurches the knight to b5 — a serious inaccuracy.
We simply capture on b5 with the bishop; White has blundered the knight.
White plays f3.
The bishop returns to d3.
White's king wanders to g3, and we plant a rook on a1.
White grabs the c-pawn, and we recapture with the bishop, capturing on c2 — up two full rooks now.
White's king shuffles to f2.
We double the rooks again, the back one to a2.
White's king goes back to g3, and the bishop snaps the pawn, capturing on e4.
White tries the bishop to h3.
We finish it — the rook captures on f3, checkmate. A classic, smooth King's Indian win.
We answer the king's pawn with c5 — the Sicilian, heading for the Najdorf.
We continue with d6.
White opens the centre with d4 — the Open Sicilian.
We capture on d4.
White recaptures with the knight and we develop our knight to f6. After White's knight to c3 we'd have several roads — ...g6 for the Dragon, ...Nc6 for the Classical, ...e6, or ...e5.
White develops the knight to c3.
The Najdorf's signature move: a6, dear to every Sicilian player. Its first point is simple — it covers b5, keeping White's knight and bishop off that square.

White chooses the bishop to e2 — a very popular reply, and White's quietest. But "quiet" is relative: the position stays sharp. It's called quiet because here White castles short, whereas in the bishop-g5 and bishop-b3 systems White castles long and both sides storm opposite wings.
We play e5. To an outsider this looks bizarre — if it doesn't strike you as strange, you're missing something. ...e6 would give the Scheveningen; the ...e5 Najdorf is our choice.

White retreats the knight to b3. Now, why does ...e5 look like a blunder? It weakens the d6-pawn and, above all, the d5-square. This is exactly why the Najdorf isn't for beginners — you're breaking basic positional rules, and you only earn that right once you truly know them. There's no single reason ...e5 holds up; it's a web of them, and the first is the most basic: we get on with development.

We develop the bishop to e7 — the main move, readying quick castling; the c8-bishop may later fianchetto to b7. Here's the first strand of the web: we have a crowd of pieces to fight for the d5-square.

White castles. Concretely: our bishop can go to e6 and the f6-knight be backed up by its partner from d7 — two pieces directly and one indirectly guarding d5, so White can rarely plant a knight there and make it stick.

We castle. The second strand: we get counterplay on both wings, the ...b5 advance in particular offsetting the d5 weakness. Even so, the hole is real — a knight that lands on d5 and stays can decide the game, so it must be respected, never ignored.
We take White; Black answers our king's pawn with ...e5.
We develop the knight to f3; Black defends with ...Nc6.
We play the Italian bishop to c4.
Black mirrors with ...Bc5 — the Giuoco Piano.
We prepare the d4 break with c3.
Black develops the knight to f6.
We strike with d4.
Black takes on d4.
We recapture on d4.
Black checks with the bishop to b4.
We block with the bishop to d2.
Black grabs on e4 with the knight — the main line.
We develop the knight to c3, offering the piece.
Black trades on d2; we recapture with the knight.
Black castles.
We castle.
Black snatches on d4 with the knight.
We play a3, hitting the bishop.
Black takes our knight, capturing on c3.
We recapture with the b-pawn.
Black retreats the knight to c6.
We play the rook to e1.
Black strikes with d5.
We retreat the bishop to f1.
Black develops the bishop to e6.
We reroute the knight to f3.
Black plays the queen to f6.
We play the rook to b1.
Black plays b6.
We take Black and answer the king's pawn with e5 — back to our roots.
We develop the knight to c6.
White plays d4 — the Scotch.
We capture on d4.
White recaptures with the knight — the pure Scotch.
We choose the bishop to c5 — still theoretical, but more manageable than the chaos of the ...Nf6 lines.
White develops the bishop to e3.
The main move: the queen to f6, piling pressure on the d4-knight.
We take White. Today is a defensive lesson — we're going to sacrifice a knight on purpose and show how to fight on when down material.
We develop the knight to c3, a Three Knights setup.
Black develops the bishop to c5. Our plan: sacrifice the knight — but not just yet.
We develop the bishop to c4.
Black plays d6.
Here's the sacrifice — the knight takes on e5, giving up the piece for at least a pawn.
Black recaptures, dxe5. Objectively we're a piece down and lost — but development isn't finished, so the plan is to complete it and make Black work for the win.
We play d3, part of finishing development — castle next, then start thinking in earnest.
Black plays the queen to f6, going for mate — and honestly that's encouraging: this walks into our hands.
We castle, defending f2. The trouble with the queen on f6 is that it invites a later knight to d5.

Black guards the square with the knight to e7. Now, the best defensive moves both improve your position and set a trap. The bishop to e3 is logical — if Black trades, we retake with the f-pawn and hit f7 from two sources. But there's something sharper: after the bishop to b3, Black plays ...Bb6 and comes to regret it.
We want f4 to prise open the f-file for chances — so first the king steps to h1, the classic preparation.
Black castles, and we're ready for f4.
We push f4, opening the file and stirring real intrigue on the kingside — the first progress in our counterplay.
Black captures on f4.
We must recapture with the bishop. Taking with the rook tempts you — it hits the queen — but attacking the queen isn't automatically good: the rook on f4 would be badly placed.
Black plays the queen to g6. Remember we're only a piece down — win three pawns for it and material is level.
So we take on c7 with the bishop, snapping off a pawn — pawns like that don't lie by the roadside.
Black pins with the bishop to g4. We must move the queen — to d2, or the interesting e1 to drag it toward the kingside.
The queen goes to d2. I avoid e1 because it runs into the knight rerouting to d4, and we want c2 guarded; from d2 the queen can also swing to f4 later.
Black jumps the knight to d4 — but it no longer carries a threat and hands us a free tempo.
We play the cryptic bishop to e5, pressing the knight on d4 — hoping Black obliges with the knight from e7 to c6.
Black finds the queen to h5 instead — a different, even stronger way of hitting our e5-bishop.
We drop the bishop back to g3 — where it was headed anyway, off the awkward c7-square and out of tactical trouble.
Black plays the knight to g6. My trick failed — yet it half-worked, because moving that knight has the same effect I was after.
Here's why I wanted that knight off e7: it guarded d5. Now we plant the knight on d5 and start building central pressure.
We were eyeing c3 next — but Black finds the knight to e2, a really nasty shot I missed. The bishop to f2 would defend, but ...Bd6 keeps the pressure; our emergency resource is the queen to e1.
So the queen to e1, forced — Black is playing superbly; that knight leap completely escaped me.
The knight takes on g3 with check — it was a mating threat — and we recapture with the queen. The trade actually helps us: Black has thinned his own attack, and now h3 is coming.
Black brings a rook to d8, setting a threat. We have two pawns for the piece — consolidate and we hold real chances.
The threat was ...Bd6, skewering the queen with mate to follow — so h3 must come at once, blunting it; if Black tries ...Bd6 anyway, we simply take the bishop on g4.
Black retreats the bishop to e6. Our sole trump is the central pawn mass Black doesn't have, so we must expand there.
We play c3, preparing to roll the centre with d4 and later e4–e5.
Black plays the bishop to d6. We're in deep trouble — ...Qe5 next is a serious problem.
We try the queen to f2 — a long shot, hoping to bait a sacrifice on h3.
Black takes the bait, sacrificing on h3.
We recapture, gxh3 — and I can't quite see where Black's mate is.
Black checks on h3, our king goes to g1 — and ...Nh4 is a bolt from the blue, threatening ...Nf3 with check and a mating net.

But there may be a defence. The knight lands on h4 threatening ...Nf3, which works only by pulling our queen off f2 — so we sidestep the queen. And here c3 pays off: a bishop to c5 now would allow d4, so if ...Nf3 comes we take it with the rook and keep control of h2. Black has a perpetual for a draw if he wants it — I'd gladly take that; what would truly worry me is a slow strengthening move like ...Re8.
We open with e4, and Black springs the Alekhine, the knight to f6.
We go for maximum space, chasing the knight with e5.
The knight jumps in to d5.
We build the big centre with d4 — heading for the Four Pawns Attack.
Black strikes at our centre with d6.
We keep grabbing space with c4, kicking the knight again.
The knight retreats to b6. The classical main line is to take on d6, but there's a far more ambitious road.
The Four Pawns Attack — f4, propping up e5. It's central domination, and if White doesn't know it, White can get crushed in five moves.
Black strikes first, capturing on e5.
We recapture on e5 with the f-pawn — a giant centre, but we've fallen behind in development.
Black develops the knight to c6. The automatic knight-to-f3 here is a serious inaccuracy because of the bishop to g4.
Rather than c5, which would gift the d5 outpost, we defend the centre with the bishop to e3.
Black develops the bishop to f5.
We develop the knight to c3, so a later knight-to-b4 can be met with the rook to c1.
Black lines the queen up on d7.
Now that we're developed, the knight to f3 is safe — the bishop-g4 pin no longer bites.
Black pins the f3-knight with the bishop to g4 anyway.
Black castles queenside instead of grabbing the pawn.
The engine's idea — c5. With Black castled queenside, giving up d5 is worth it: c5 clamps down and jump-starts our own attack.
Black posts the knight on d5.
We take on d5.
Black recaptures with the queen, capturing on d5.
Artemis-style — the king to f2, guarding the bishop, connecting the rooks, and preparing the queen to a4.
Black solidifies with e6.
The queen to a4 is tempting, but first we tickle with h3 — so if the bishop ever comes to h5, we have g4 in our pocket.
The bishop drops instead to f5, a little unexpected.
Out comes the queen to a4, and Black answers with the queen to e4, eyeing our c5-pawn.
We sidestep the queen to a3, Black slots the queen into c2, and we push b4, insisting on the attack.
Black tucks the bishop to e7, and we roll on with b5.
The knight is forced back to b8 — so we can simply grab the a7-pawn.

We push to g7 and set the queen toward h5, sowing doubt. This game is really about recovery technique when you're lost, and the principles are these. Complicate — pose your opponent decision after decision, because decisions breed fatigue and doubt. Keep your pieces active — bring the rook in with h4 rather than a timid g3, and ask the "Shankland question": what happens if you just do it anyway, developing and ignoring a pawn? Defend key pawns by developing, not by a passive king move — a rook to d3 both guards c3 and prepares to lift to g3. Manoeuvre the knight toward a dream square like d6, via f7. Use a break like d5 not only to lure the bishop off b7 but to open lines and strip away defenders. And once you win material back, convert with a passed pawn — push it hard while the opponent is passive, escort it with a rook cutting off the king, and finish with the ladder-mate technique, bringing your own king up to guard the checking square so the rooks can deliver mate. Even dead lost, purposeful, problem-posing play saves a remarkable number of games.

Black plays the knight to c6, and here a rule worth remembering: an idea that failed in one position can suddenly work in another — now d5 is strong, a tempo push on the knight that also denies Black the time for the blockading ...Bd6. Prevent ...Bd6 with the bishop to f4, since that bishop is Black's only way to blockade the passed pawn — kept out, the passer becomes a huge asset. A few threads run through the finish: when you're a pawn up, unlike a piece up, you generally do NOT want to trade queens, as it relieves the defender; the g5-pin is dangerous, all the more with the queen already eyeing the knight; and combinations are built by stacking threats — a capture on f6 opens the g-file for a queen check on g3, while a rook to d1 x-rays the queen, so a discovered check wins material. Principled development plus these small, flexible observations is what makes strong players win almost automatically.

Here's the whole reason the Caro exists: unlike the French, we get to develop this light-squared bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain, to f5, before we ever shut it in with e6 — and that's exactly what we've done. White answers with f4, grabbing more central space, but it's not a good move: it curbs the development of White's own light bishop and it weakens his king.
The proper reply is e6 — White has over-committed his pawns while lagging in development.

White develops the bishop to d3. Since this is our first Advance Caro, here's the rationale. The centre is CLOSED, and a closed centre is built of pawn chains — our black pawns form one chain, and d4 with e5 is White's chain. The side with more levers, more ability to attack and undermine the OTHER side's chain, is the side holding the initiative — and the whole point of the Caro is that Black is that side. When your opponent plays passively, the textbook punishment is to open the centre — so d4 is the perfect opportunity, unless I'm missing something tactical.

The knight to g3, for two reasons: first, more king safety; second, I'm already thinking about knight sallies like the knight to h5. And note the bishop takes h3 is not a move, because the knight defends it — but whenever the f-file is open like this, always watch for the bishop takes h3. Black is clearly worse; he missed the bishop takes g8 and has insufficient compensation.

If Black plays the bishop to e6, the natural move is the knight to d4, centralizing and hitting the bishop — but that walks into c5, so it's not desirable yet. He plays the bishop to c5, setting up threats on the diagonal.

We could play the bishop to e3 to trade bishops, at the cost of our structure; or a neutral c3 to prepare b4, where he'd answer a5. I don't like the bishop to g5, which walks into the queen to b6 and a battery on b2. Actually, I think the best move is the bishop to e3.

So a more indirect approach — a5 weakens the b5 square.

The bishop to b5 has limited value since Black plays e6, so I like the Alapin-esque idea of getting the knight to b5. So the knight to a3 — from b5 the knight eyes c7, and if Black pushes the e-pawn and we play the knight to b5, we can even reach d6, where after Black takes and we recapture, we get the bishop pair and dark-square control; even if Black wins the pawn back, we'd get the better endgame. A nice flexible developing move, waiting for Black to show his cards.

The knight to c6 is one of the most common responses, but it's already a serious inaccuracy — not quite a mistake if Black follows up correctly, but one more slip and things get disastrously bad within five or six moves.
Our response is obvious: c3 prepared d4, and the knight to c6 doesn't stop it — we have enough defenders — so we grab the centre with d4.
Black takes, capturing on d4. The knight to c6 is misplaced here for a simple reason.

We recapture with a pawn, capturing on d4, threatening to push to d5 — and without a pawn shell to support them, Black's pieces get tossed around with no central footholds and can even be trapped. After d5 and the knight to e5, f4 sends the knight all the way back to g6, and the knight to f6 is even worse: after d5, the knight to e5, f4, the knight to g6, e5, the knight has only g8, since g4 and h5 are covered by our queen. A justified violation of opening principles — moving only pawns, but with tempo.

So we either push our own pawn to d5, grabbing the centre and chasing the knight, or just develop with the knight to c3 and the knight to f3. Black plays d5 — and the instinct is to meet it with e5, but that's inaccurate: unlike the Advance French, where Black's pawn is already on e6 giving the bad French bishop, here Black gets a good French or Caro-Kann, bringing the bishop out to f5 first and only then locking with e6.
So we take, capturing on d5, rather than allow that improved French.
The queen recaptures on d5 — transposing into a line normally reached via a different move order, and this is an isolated-queen-pawn structure.
We're playing the King's Indian — the knight to f6.
The bishop to g5 — the Trompowsky, named after the Brazilian Octavio Trompowsky. There's a misconception that only the knight to e4 works here; actually Black has many ways to equalize.
e6 and even g6 are reasonable, d5 is underrated, even c5 is playable — but I've always played the principled knight to e4.

At a lower level, h4 — the Hodgson variation, a very double-edged move — causes consternation. Its idea is simple: it defends the bishop, and if Black takes on g5, White recaptures with the h-pawn, opening the h-file (Black has the h7 pawn, restricting the rook) and creating a deep-freeze — the g5 pawn making it very hard for Black to ever fix the h7 weakness, since after h6 White takes and damages Black's kingside. So taking the bishop isn't best.

Black has many options; I'll play it simply with d5 — occupy the centre and toss the ball back. h4's drawback, beyond not developing, is that it commits White to an uncertain king: kingside castling is unlikely with the damage, queenside is risky with the knight on e4, and staying central is dubious.

The knight to d2 — he knows his theory. I don't want to take on g5, which plays into White's hands; instead I'll simply drop the knight back to f6 or d6, a symmetrical Queen's-Gambit-Declined-type position.
The knight back to f6. Moving the same piece three times seems wrong, but the centre is closed, so the effect is diminished — and White spent tempi on the weakening h4.

e3. The point of the knight's to-and-fro: we induced h4, provoking a serious kingside weakness, and now develop conventionally. We've been move-ordered into a reverse Queen's Gambit Declined — where White plays c4, we play c5 from the black side, but after c5 we must watch d takes c5.
Since White is developed, after c5, d takes c5, e6, White solidifies with b4 — so we start with the solid e6 and follow with c5 to contest and pressure White's centre.

The knight to e2. Let's play c5 — we can also throw in h6 to force the bishop to commit, but no rush; this pin isn't dangerous, since an easy test is whether the pinned piece is protected by a pawn, and it is.
We play c5, and White takes, capturing on c5.
We recapture with the bishop, capturing on c5 — precisely why we started with e6.
White's knights on e2 and d2 are passive; a3 is a good move, preparing b4. Many would auto-play a5, but not every idea must be prevented — b4 isn't a threat, just an idea; what does b4 actually do?

b4 chases our bishop from c5 — but the bishop is happy to drop to e7, ending the pin. So we develop the knight to c6. And after b4, that pawn becomes a target: we chisel with a5 once White's pawn is on b4 — the base of the chain, or sometimes the tip.
The knight to f4 — a perfect chance for the move I mentioned earlier: the bishop on g5 is now fully deprived of squares.
So it's time for h6, forcing White to trade the bishop for the knight, capturing on f6, letting our queen come to the active f6.
We recapture with the queen, capturing on f6. White has traded the dark-squared bishop, the pride of the Trompowsky — a great position for us.

The queen on f6 attacks b2 and pressures f2 — Black's already better. The knight to h5. We can grab the pawn on b2: people fear the queen getting trapped, but calculate concretely — after the queen takes b2, the rook to b1, our queen defends g7, so we drop it to e5, not c3 where the rook to b3 chases it; the central queen looks vulnerable to f4, but f4 gives up e3 with check.

The queen takes, capturing on b2. After the rook to b1, the queen to e5 — and if White chases with the knight, it severs the connection to the h5-knight, letting us take on h5. So we can safely take b2. Even if e5 were unavailable, taking on a3 would be fine — a king move to f8 isn't the end of the world.
The bishop to e2. We have ways to deal with g7 — g6 is the forcing option, or we simply castle. The king is safest on f8, surrounded by pawn cover; d7 walks into the d-file x-ray.

Castling kills two birds — it develops and protects g7. If I were White I'd contemplate g4 for kingside counterplay, using the uncastled king: the trope where the uncastled side can benefit from the h1-rook if the h-file opens — see Vukovic's Art of Attack.

My recommendation is the Accelerated Dragon. White surprises with c4 — think of it as an English where White plays c4, we play c5, and White plays e4. Its drawback jumps out: White has created a massive hole on d4 — a square no pawn can ever defend, since the c- and e-pawns have advanced past it.

This gives our knight a potential outpost on d4 — but a hole existing doesn't mean occupy it at once. We start with the knight to c6, not to play the knight to d4 next: it's too early, with nothing else developed.
The knight to f3 would just knock a d4-knight off. It's the long-term weakness that costs White later. We also get a massive diagonal for our dark-squared bishop.
We play g6 — though in a classical game I'd prefer e6 or the knight to f6, since g6 allows White to transition to main lines.
The drawback of g6: it allows d4 — after d4, c takes d4, knight takes d4, we transpose to the Maroczy Bind Accelerated Dragon. Since we're emphasizing openings, I wouldn't mind. White plays d3.
After the bishop to g7, we're flat-out better: great pieces, dominating the dark squares, and White's light bishop is now a big pawn.

The knight to c3. We develop normally. It's self-evidently good to trade our light bishop for White's f3-knight — visualize it gone: our control of d4 increases, and we can contemplate the knight to d4, though White can still trade it with the dark bishop or the c3-knight, both awkward.
The best way to threaten that trade is d6 — a normal developing move I like more than the knight to f6, which I'll delay. White plays the bishop to e3.
We develop the bishop to g4, continuing to clamp d4, trading a piece that controls it — classic positional chess.
The bishop to e2. Do we take on f3 or wait? It doesn't matter — both are good.
I'll eliminate the knight while we can, capturing on f3 — the drawback of waiting is that the knight could move away.
White recaptures, capturing on f3.

The Botvinnik setup: fianchetto the dark bishop, then carve a square for the g8-knight with e6, keeping the bishop unobstructed. The e6 pawn is an asset, controlling d5 and f5 — a toothy central construction.
We take White and open e4; Black replies e6 — the French. This is our opening-focused run: play principled moves and punish typical non-theoretical setups.
We build the big centre with d4.
Black plays the offbeat ...Nc6 rather than the main ...d5. Don't assume a non-theoretical move means you're already winning; just develop soundly.
We simply develop the knight to f3 — an immediate ...d5 is too concrete before we've developed.
Black plays the passive ...d6. We have several ways to punish it; the simplest is the knight to c3, keeping to the spirit of e4 openings rather than grabbing space with c4.
We develop the knight to c3.
Black develops the knight to f6.

The bishop comes to d3 — it props up e4, and once Black castles short we can push e5 and aim the bishop at h7. Combined with the queen coming to e4, that battery threatens mate on h7. Note: even if Black plays ...h6, the square itself stays weak — don't confuse a weak pawn with a weak square.

Black plays ...h6 and we castle. We're unbothered by ...Nb4 — the bishop just steps back and a3 chases it. Black's slow queenside play neglects his kingside, which we punish by opening the centre: Black's d6- and e6-pawns are hooks, and a pawn advance can act like dynamite to blow the centre open.

Black plays ...b6, and we strike with d5 — the thematic dynamiting of the centre, and crucially it opens the e-file straight at Black's king. If Black takes, we have two defenders to his two attackers; we'd play it even as a sacrifice, because that file is the highway to the king — which is exactly why we castled early.
Black captures on d5.
We recapture with the pawn — a major step toward winning.

Black plays ...Nb4. Our objective now is to keep Black's king stuck in the centre — a moving target is hard to hit. We can't stop ...Be7, but a rook to e1 with check pins it, and by piling pressure on the pinned bishop we keep the king glued to the centre as a defender.
First we insert the check on b5 — avoiding a trade and keeping our light-squared bishop, which rakes the light squares that ...b6 weakened.
